finding: The live range of $80-$440 is slightly low at the bottom and too low at the top for any job done with a genuine (dealer) motor; it is about right for an ordinary vehicle fitted with an aftermarket motor. Built totals use parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks). Economy, 2015 Honda Fit: $67.99 aftermarket to $641.13 genuine + 0.3-1.0 hr = about $104-$801 (aftermarket motor about $104-$228; genuine motor about $677-$801). Midsize, 2022 Honda Pilot front blower: $67.44 to $346.52 + 0.4-1.0 hr = about $115-$507 (aftermarket about $115-$227; genuine about $395-$507). Truck, 2016 Silverado 1500: $59.99 to $336.96 + 0.4-1.0 hr = about $108-$497 (aftermarket about $108-$220; genuine about $385-$497). Luxury, 2016 Acura RLX: no aftermarket motor was found, so the low is the lowest online price seen for the genuine Acura motor, not an aftermarket price: $624.95 discounted to $1,117.99 at list + 0.3-0.9 hr = about $661-$1,262 (discounted genuine motor about $661-$769; at list about $1,154-$1,262). So the lowest totals we can build are about $104-$115, above the live $80, and they assume the cheapest motor at a dealer warranty time; Jerry's low figure is $130. A floor nearer $110-$130 is better supported. With an aftermarket motor every example lands under about $230, well inside the live range, and RepairPal's national average ($383-$435) sits at the live top. But a genuine motor alone lists at $337 to $1,118 on these four vehicles, so dealer-part jobs run from about $385 to past $1,200, well over $440. Online discounted genuine prices ($163-$783, and $625 at one seller for the RLX motor) are far below list, which is why quotes vary so much. Nothing is left null, but the RLX low is not like the other three: retailer pages for that car showed genuine parts only and two more searches found no aftermarket motor, so its low is a discounted genuine part ($624.95) and an RLX owner should not expect the under-$230 totals the other examples reach. How solid the labor times are: the low ends for the Fit and RLX (0.3 hr) and the Pilot (0.4 hr) are Honda/Acura warranty flat-rate times printed in dealer bulletins for the example vehicles themselves; a warranty time is the low end of what a shop bills. The truck's 0.4 hr comes from a Honda Ridgeline bulletin, not a full-size truck. The high ends are weak. No source was found stating a shop time for the Fit, Pilot or RLX: the 1.0 hr used for economy and midsize is a parts retailer's approximate install time for the Silverado (the truck example, where it does apply), and the luxury 0.9 hr is a named mechanic's quoted flat-rate time for a 2002 Mercedes E320. A forum post saying 'around an hour on average' points the same way but is weak evidence. So four of the eight hour figures are not for the example vehicle. These times fit vehicles with easy under-dash access; forum reports loaded here mention about 4 hours on a 2008-2013 Nissan Rogue and 8-10 hours on unnamed cars, and RepairPal notes that some vehicles need the dash removed, so hard-access vehicles cost far more than any total above. One caution on the economy low: the $67.99 Fit motor is a seller's own-brand part, not a named major brand. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee (the same symptoms can come from a blower resistor or power module, a fuse, a relay or the control head), the blower resistor or module itself when it has failed or been overheated by the old motor, a cabin air filter (Honda's own bulletins replace the filter with the motor), shop supplies and sales tax. Three-row vehicles have a separate rear blower that is quoted separately.
